ab.summary:
Infrastructure engineer with 26 years in the field in the public sector — from the first network security architectures to sovereign on-premise AI platforms. My career spans operational systems security (antivirus, firewall, DMZ, security policy), the management of complex IT projects in a COFRAC-certified environment, and the building of fully open source on-premise AI infrastructures. I prefer to remain the go-to technical expert — the one who builds, documents, and shares what he learns.

This portfolio is the open demonstration of that work: whether you are looking to hire this profile, to have a sovereign AI infrastructure designed for your organization, to discuss your own project, or simply to draw inspiration from what is proven feasible — it is all documented here.

ab.philo.text: Everything presented in this portfolio is built with free tools. Git, Proxmox VE, Docker, Python, Ollama, PostgreSQL, pgvector, Nextcloud, MariaDB, nginx, Obsidian — every technical choice has an open source alternative. It is not a constraint: it is a conviction. Code transparency, the community that maintains it, and data sovereignty are values I defend as much in my personal projects as in my professional ones. This portfolio is a reference guide shared freely — because documenting and passing on knowledge is part of the job.

idx.pres.box:
Context: Design of a high-performance local AI platform based on Proxmox VE, an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU in VFIO passthrough, Windows/Linux virtualization, ZFS storage, Docker infrastructure, hosting of local LLMs (Ollama), vector RAG (PostgreSQL/pgvector), n8n automation and multimodal tools (Whisper, ComfyUI).

Purpose: to demonstrate that an organization — a local authority (town hall) or an SME — can host its own AI and automation services while remaining sovereign over its infrastructure and data. Some building blocks are in production, others validated on the design platform or being deployed.

infrastructure → virtualization → deployment → AI operations, built entirely on open source tools.

vm302.desc: VM302 — a polyglot Windows 11 development workstation (VSCodium, Python 3.13, Node.js 24 LTS) evaluating programming assistants with DeepSeek Harness, consuming remote GPU inference hosted separately. Portfolio of Stéphane Muraro.
vm302.subtitle: Windows 11 · VSCodium · Python 3.13 · Node.js 24 LTS · DeepSeek Harness · remote GPU inference
vm302.intro: VM302 is a Windows 11 development workstation dedicated to polyglot development and the evaluation of programming assistants. The machine has no local GPU: it consumes a separately hosted inference capacity, which separates the client workstation from the compute service.
vm302.p1.list:
• Virtualized Windows 11 base, without a local GPU accelerator
  • VSCodium, Git and PowerShell 7 validated through functional tests
  • Guest identity, network, guest agent and peripherals re-validated
  • Python 3.13 — package management, virtual environment, offline test of standard libraries
  • Node.js 24 LTS and npm — running a local JavaScript test
  • DeepSeek Harness in a pinned preliminary version: lockfile, package integrity, dependency audit, install scripts and native modules checked
  • Harness interface limited to the local machine, first profile kept read-only
vm302.p2.list:
• First validated remote inference with qwen3.6:35b: the control prompt returned exactly DSH_VM302_QWEN36_OK, with no tool call
  • After a reboot of the machine: versions, configuration and session history persisted
  • New session confirming the expected response and remote GPU acceleration
  • Access to the inference service limited to the private network, with no direct publication of its API on the Internet
  • Automation services checked at the health level, without yet declaring consumption by an agent
vm302.arch.label: separation between the dev workstation and the inference service

├── VSCodium · Git · PowerShell 7

vm302.arch.p: The workstation stays lightweight and GPU-less: compute is delegated to a separately hosted inference service, reachable only on the private network. This separation isolates the development tooling from the model service.

  • Design of a polyglot development toolchain

  • Reproducible tests and offline validation

infra.skills:
• High-performance local AI server architecture
  • Hardware selection for GPU inference (VRAM, bandwidth)
  • CPU / RAM sizing for a multi-VM hypervisor
  • BIOS/UEFI configuration for virtualization and PCIe passthrough
  • High-performance NVMe storage management with ZFS
infra.notes:
Principle: the GPU is assigned directly to the VMs that need it; GPU workloads (VM210) and shared CPU services (VM215) are kept separate to limit dependencies and ease backups.

Industrialization: the VMs are derived from generic and CUDA templates, customized via Cloud-Init; rebuilding them follows a reversible procedure (a control clone is validated before any replacement).

Limitations: a diagnostic 400 W software cap was used previously (versus 600 W by default); the latest ComfyUI/Ollama tests were run at 600 W, with no guarantee of long-term stability nor an established performance comparison (procedure on the AI & LLM page). ZFS snapshots also ease technical rollbacks but do not replace an independent backup — that policy is still being defined.
prox.title: Proxmox VE — On-Premise AI Portfolio
prox.why: Why Proxmox for this project? The hypervisor is the base that makes the platform scalable and agile: each role (AI node, shared services, PoC bench) is added, isolated or evolves without touching the others. It brings a real time saving — in case of corruption, an entire server is recloned in a few minutes from a template or a snapshot, instead of reinstalling everything. And it extends the possibilities: Linux / Windows coexistence on the same machine, including one or more Windows clients to consume the AI services, with GPU allocation on demand.

prox.startup.intro: This command produces directly from Proxmox the list of VMs with their current state, their auto-start policy (onboot) and their resume order (startup) — without confusing the instantaneous state (running / stopped) with the persistent configuration.
prox.startup.label2: sanitized excerpt — resume order: VM215 (10) → VM210 (20) → VM300 n8n (30) → VM205 (40)
prox.startup.notes: Reading: VMs with onboot=1 resume in increasing startup order — VM215 (services · PostgreSQL/pgvector) → VM210 (AI node) → VM300 (n8n) → VM205 (Nextcloud) — so that dependencies are ready before their consumers. Alternative GPU environments stay out of auto-start. The exhaustive inventory remains in the internal operations documentation.

prox.p5.body:
Cloning an old template revealed a residual hostname. The clone was fixed and checked, then the generic template was rebuilt from an official ISO to explicitly control its content. The build VM was sanitized before conversion: machine identity, hostname, SSH keys, network, Cloud-Init state and logs were cleaned.

A full validation clone confirmed Cloud-Init initialization, generation of a clean identity, networking, DNS, SSH, the guest agent, and persistence after reboot. The old template was only replaced after this check; the ZFS origins were verified before deleting the candidate that had become redundant, to preserve VM independence.
prox.lifecycle.intro: A template is not worth much for its cloning speed but for the mastery of what it transmits (system, identity, network, access, initialization). Building, validating and replacing are three separate operations: the old template stays available until its replacement and its validation clone have met every criterion.
prox.lifecycle.label: template lifecycle
prox.t3: Base typeExpected contentExcluded elementsGeneric serverminimal system, Cloud-Init, SSH, guest agentapplication, secret, business configurationSpecialized servergeneric base + justified common dependenciesdata specific to one VMCUDA / GPUvalidated GPU drivers and toolsapplication unrelated to the GPUWindowsprepared system, VirtIO drivers, generalization mechanismidentity and account specific to the source VM
prox.lifecycle.notes: A specialized template must not make the generic one dependent on its components; applications normally stay installed in the clones.
prox.pcie.body: An onboard PCIe device intermittently disappeared. The diagnosis distinguished a real absence on the bus from a simple driver fault, by successively checking the interface, the modules, PCIe enumeration, the parent port and the rescan. A full power cycle restored the device; recurrence is being monitored before considering a conditional firmware update.
rp.title: Reverse Proxy VM200 — HTTPS Publishing | On-Premise AI Portfolio
rp.desc: VM200 — shared Nginx reverse proxy: HTTPS publishing of OpenWebUI, n8n and Nextcloud, TLS termination, virtual hosts, Certbot and Fail2ban. Portfolio of Stéphane Muraro.
rp.intro: VM200 is the Web entry point of the self-hosted infrastructure. It publishes applications installed on other machines without directly exposing their internal ports to the Internet. It receives HTTPS connections, presents the public certificate, selects the requested service and relays the request to the right machine on the local network.
rp.deployed:
• Dedicated Linux VM from an Ubuntu Server template
  • Nginx as the reverse proxy
  • Let's Encrypt certificates managed by Certbot
  • Active local firewall
  • Fail2ban active and validated for SSH administration
  • HTTP → HTTPS redirection and certificate renewal tested
  • Streaming responses and WebSocket connections validated
  • VM200 restart validated with no configuration loss
rp.t1: ServicePublic statusOpenWebUI · VM210🟢 published & HTTPS validatedn8n · VM300🟢 published & HTTPS validatedNextcloud · VM205🟢 published & HTTPS validatedother internal services⚪ not published / deferred
rp.p3.h: 🧭 From a domain name to another machine
rp.path.p1: DNS only associates the public name with the Internet address — it does not know which VM hosts the application. The router does not choose the service either: it hands Web connections off to VM200. It is Nginx that performs the application-level routing: the name requested during the TLS negotiation and in the HTTP request selects a configuration block (virtual host) that designates the target internal machine and service.
rp.path.label2: several public names, one Internet connection
rp.dns.notes: The existence of a DNS record does not prove that a service is published: a virtual host, a valid certificate, an authorized backend and a test from an external network are also required.
rp.t2: ComponentResponsibilityLimitPublic DNSassociate a name with the Internet addressdoes not choose the internal VMRouterforward Web traffic to VM200does not understand the applicationsVM200 firewallreject unplanned inbound connectionsdoes not replace authenticationNginxterminate HTTPS, select the virtual host, relaydoes not store business dataCertbotobtain/renew Let's Encrypt certificatesdoes not publish an application by itselfFail2banblock certain repetitive attacks from the logsreplaces neither a firewall nor strong passwordsBackendserve the application, control its usersmust not be exposed directly
rp.tls.p1: Public encryption terminates on VM200. The certificate and its private key stay centralized on the reverse proxy, which avoids managing a different public certificate on each backend.
rp.tls.p2: Nginx forwards the requested name, the external protocol and the information needed for traceability to the backend. For interactive applications, it supports WebSockets, streaming responses and timeouts suited to long-running processing.
rp.defense.list:
• the router only sends VM200 the necessary Web traffic
  • the local firewall rejects other inbound connections
  • administration stays limited to the internal network
  • Nginx only relays configured names and services
  • TLS encrypts and authenticates the public connection
  • Fail2ban reduces certain observable repetitive attempts
  • each backend keeps its own authentication and filtering
  • databases and technical APIs stay absent from the WAN
rp.defense.note: Fail2ban is validated for SSH; this does not automatically protect application login forms — each protection requires an exploitable log and a tested filter.
rp.publish.list:
• validate the service on the local network
  • identify its HTTPS, WebSocket, request size and timeout needs
  • define its public name and authentication model
  • configure the application for its public origin
  • create a separate virtual host on VM200
  • validate the Nginx syntax before reloading
  • obtain and test the certificate
  • test from a genuinely external network
  • check the logs and the absence of direct exposure
  • document the rollback
rp.rollback:
↩️ Rollback — three levels:
  • disable only the virtual host of one service;
  • temporarily remove the Web forwarding to VM200;
  • stop VM200 to neutralize all publications without changing the internal applications.

The formal test of the global rollback by removing the WAN forwarding remains the last open check of the first phase.
rp.skills.final:
• Design of a shared reverse proxy
  • DNS, NAT, SNI, virtual hosts and proxy headers
  • Automation of the certificate lifecycle
  • Support for WebSockets and streaming
  • Segmentation between the Internet boundary and backends
  • Defense in depth and rollback strategy
  • Publishing a service hosted on another machine

gpu.notes1: ⚠️ Advanced skill: GPU Passthrough VFIO is one of the most complex and sought-after achievements in the portfolio. It allows the RTX 5090 to be physically assigned to a VM, with performance close to a native installation.
gpu.notes2: Why an RTX 5090 for local AI? With its CUDA and Tensor cores and its 32 GB of GDDR7 memory, it strongly accelerates the parallel computation needed for language model inference, embeddings and image generation — while keeping the models and processed data local.
gpu.notes3: Why passthrough despite its constraints? PCIe passthrough with VFIO directly assigns the card to a VM: the guest system, CUDA and containers use the GPU with near-native performance and clear workload isolation. In return, the assignment is exclusive (no simultaneous use by several VMs) and requires rigorous preparation of the host, boot process and recovery procedures.
gpu.power.p1: A temporary 400 W software cap (versus 600 W by default on the observed card) was used during an electrical diagnostic. The ComfyUI and Ollama tests of September 27–28, 2026 were then run at 600 W, by explicit decision. No lasting stability gain nor performance comparison between these caps has been established.
gpu.power.label: reproducible public check
gpu.power.p2: The 400 W diagnostic value is applied with sudo nvidia-smi --power-limit=400 — a setting that is not persistent after a reboot or driver reload. Detailed commands, telemetry and the return to the factory cap are documented on the AI & LLM (VM210) page.

gpu.p5.h: 🔄 GPU exclusivity — VM status and startup order
gpu.excl.p1: Run on the Proxmox host, this command detects the RTX 5090 (without displaying its address), identifies the VMs configured to use it, and outputs a sanitized label — distinguishing the VM's current state from its auto-start policy, and checking that only one passthrough VM is active at a time.
gpu.excl.notes: Reading: only one passthrough VM (IA-Core / VM210) uses the RTX 5090; alternative GPU environments stay out of auto-start. On host resume, VM215 (PostgreSQL/pgvector) starts first, then VM210 (GPU workload + Ollama / OpenWebUI / RAG) — with no contention for the GPU.
gpu.bios.body: A reference BIOS baseline separates values actually observed from improvements merely considered. Before any firmware update, the parameters needed for IOMMU and VFIO are backed up and a rollback is prepared; after the change, the IOMMU groups, the GPU reservation and VM startup are revalidated. Tests remain one change at a time, so that each effect can be clearly attributed to the modified parameter.
gpu.notes.final:
Structuring constraint: the RTX 5090 is an exclusive physical resource — only one passthrough VM can use it at a time. The architecture therefore explicitly documents the simultaneous-startup incompatibilities, and a separate virtual console is kept for recovery.

Validation: the NVIDIA driver and CUDA were validated in an Ubuntu VM, then GPU access was verified down into Docker containers (via the NVIDIA Container Toolkit).

rag.title: RAG & Vector Databases — On-Premise AI Portfolio
rag.subtitle: PostgreSQL · pgvector · bge-m3 · Open WebUI · Semantic search
rag.why: Why RAG? In OpenWebUI, RAG, or retrieval-augmented generation, lets the user query their own documents in natural language and get a contextualized, updatable answer grounded in the retrieved passages, without retraining the model.
rag.p1.h: 🧭 Why PostgreSQL / pgvector rather than Qdrant?
rag.why.p1: PostgreSQL with pgvector is chosen as the nominal backend: pgvector is one of the vector backends maintained by the OpenWebUI core team, while Qdrant is a non-core, community-maintained integration there — which increases the risk of breakage or delayed fixes on an OpenWebUI version upgrade. Qdrant remains a valid vector solution, kept as a fallback.
rag.why.p2: Another factor is storage: Qdrant's active data was not kept on the ZFS share presented to VM210 (via VirtioFS/FUSE) and had to stay on a local ext4 on the VM; PostgreSQL/pgvector has its own dedicated ext4 disk on VM215, better isolated for operations and future logical backup.
rag.arch: Distributed architecture: inference and embedding computation run on the GPU AI node (VM210, RTX 5090). Vector storage is offloaded to a GPU-less services VM (VM215) hosting PostgreSQL and pgvector. This separation limits dependencies and eases backup of the vector backend.
rag.flow:
[Documents] → [Chunking + bge-m3 Embeddings · GPU VM210] → [PostgreSQL / pgvector · VM215]
                                              ↓
[Question] → [Query embedding] → [HNSW semantic search] → [Local Ollama LLM] → [Cited answer]

vm301.desc: VM301 — an agentic development station on Ubuntu Server 24.04 running Hermes Agent and OpenCode, with inference delegated to the GPU node (Ollama / RTX 5090). Agent isolation, no local model. Portfolio of Stéphane Muraro.
vm301.subtitle: Ubuntu Server 24.04 · Hermes Agent · OpenCode · inference delegated to the GPU VM (VM210)
vm301.intro: VM301 is a Linux virtual machine dedicated to development assistants. It runs Hermes Agent and OpenCode while delegating inference to the platform's GPU VM. This separation provides an isolated agentic environment without duplicating models or using an additional GPU.
vm301.deployed:
• Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS
  • 4 vCPU, 8 GiB of memory, 64 GiB of system storage
  • Own identity from a full clone of the Ubuntu Server template
  • Cloud-Init, SSH and guest agent validated

  • Hermes Agent 0.20.6

  • Ollama's OpenAI-compatible endpoint reached from VM301

  • Real Hermes generation succeeded with qwen3.6:35b — served context of 65,536 tokens, deliberately restricted tool set

vm301.validation.note: This validation demonstrates the full chain between an isolated development agent and GPU-accelerated local inference.
vm301.arch.label: separation between the agentic workstation and the GPU node
vm301.arch.p: The client VM stays lightweight. Model storage, loading into video memory and inference optimizations remain centralized on the GPU node. The API is not published directly on the Internet and access is limited to explicitly authorized clients.

nc.title: Self-Hosted Nextcloud — On-Premise AI Portfolio
nc.desc: Self-hosted Nextcloud on Proxmox (Ubuntu VM, Docker + MariaDB) — sovereign file service, published over HTTPS behind a reverse proxy, with proof of recovery after a reboot.
nc.subtitle: Sovereign files · Proxmox · Docker · MariaDB
nc.why1: Why Nextcloud? Nextcloud provides a personal space to store, sync and share files across several devices, via a web interface and dedicated clients.
nc.why2: Why self-hosting? It keeps control over where data is stored, the update cycle and access rules. In exchange, availability, hardening, disk capacity, backups and restore testing must be handled independently.
nc.arch:
• Dedicated Ubuntu 24.04 VM for the service (VM205)
  • A Docker container for the Nextcloud application
  • A separate Docker container for MariaDB
  • Two Docker volumes separating application files and database
  • VM auto-start after priority services, then both containers resume
  • HTTPS publishing behind the shared reverse proxy (VM200)
nc.skills:
• Operating a self-hosted application in a Proxmox VM
  • Nextcloud / MariaDB application separation
  • Persistence via Docker volumes
  • Cross-diagnostics: systemd · Docker · HTTP · the occ tool
  • Building a reproducible, sanitized proof after a reboot
nc.https.p1: Nextcloud is reachable at nextcloud.stephanemuraro.fr. The service keeps its own authentication while the reverse proxy (VM200) centralizes TLS termination and relays requests to the application VM.
nc.https.label: Validated from an external network:
nc.https.list:
• establishing the HTTPS connection
  • authentication
  • browsing files
  • uploading a file via the web interface
  • syncing via the desktop client
nc.https.notes: The prior diagnostic isolated two faulty application extensions, neutralized reversibly to restore the interface and then writes, without deleting data.
nc.proof.p1: Run inside the VM, these commands automatically determine the container name and the published local port — so the proof does not depend on labels specific to the installation.
nc.proof.label2: sanitized excerpt — validation after host reboot
nc.proof.notes: Reading: occ status and the HTTP status endpoint confirm Nextcloud 33.0.0 installed, out of maintenance and with no pending database migration. The simultaneous presence of the Nextcloud and MariaDB containers after reboot demonstrates their automatic recovery.

  • Docker volumes on the VM's system disk — the planned dedicated ZFS storage is not yet mounted/used.
  • Free system disk capacity to monitor before significant data growth.
  • Independent backups and restore testing: not yet demonstrated.
  • Antivirus scanning chain to redeploy in persistent form before re-enabling its Nextcloud extension.
  • Neutralized external storage connector to replace with a compatible version or remove permanently.

n8n.desc: n8n on VM300 — workflow orchestration, external PostgreSQL, remote Ollama API, HTTPS publishing behind a reverse proxy. Portfolio of Stéphane Muraro.
n8n.subtitle: Workflow orchestration · VM300 · Docker · external PostgreSQL
n8n.intro: VM300 is an application VM dedicated to n8n: it runs automation workflows, delegates persistence to a services VM (PostgreSQL), and consumes the AI APIs of a separate GPU VM. This separation of application / data / compute lets each component evolve, be maintained and backed up on its own lifecycle.
n8n.deployed:
• Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS · Docker Engine + Compose
  • n8n 2.32.6 — pinned official image
  • Single instance, standard mode, without Redis
  • External PostgreSQL — encrypted connection, strong authentication
  • Remote Ollama API consumed by a validated workflow
  • Interface published over HTTPS by the shared reverse proxy
  • Persistence verified after container recreation and restart
n8n.security:
• Application port kept on the internal network, public interface exposed only over HTTPS
  • System filtering + controlled Docker publishing
  • Secrets and encryption key outside Compose and outside Git
  • Pinned application image
  • Dedicated PostgreSQL database and role, encrypted link
  • No direct Internet redirection to VM300
  • Public origin, secure cookies, trust limited to the reverse proxy
  • Inspection of workflows and node types used
n8n.arch.label: Docker isolation · reproducible deployment (Compose)
n8n.arch.p: n8n deliberately runs as a single instance: Redis and queue mode are not added until a need for parallelism or high availability is demonstrated — which reduces the number of components to operate.
n8n.ext1.list:
• Database reserved for the application
  • Separate application role, rights limited to what's needed
  • Encrypted connection · targeted network filtering
  • Recreating n8n deletes neither accounts nor workflows (data lives outside the container)
n8n.ext2.list:
• AI computation offloaded to the GPU node
  • VM300 calls an authorized Ollama API, with no GPU or model copy
  • Validated workflow: request preparation → HTTP call → model response → output normalization
n8n.pub.p: The editor is published over HTTPS at n8n.stephanemuraro.fr (authenticated admin interface and webhook URLs produced by the instance), behind the VM200 reverse proxy. VM300's application port is not exposed directly: every public request passes through VM200, which terminates HTTPS, selects the service by the requested name, and relays only the intended routes. A later separation under a dedicated webhook name remains possible if a need for stricter exposure is confirmed.
n8n.pub.label: path of a public request
n8n.pub.notes: n8n is aware of its public HTTPS origin, trusts the expected proxy, and uses secure cookies. Authentication, the editor, running a workflow, reconnection and persistence have been validated from the Internet (external network).
n8n.example.label: workflow (illustrative)
n8n.iac.p: Automation is not limited to n8n: the platform relies on Proxmox templates, snapshots and cloning for reproducible deployment.
n8n.iac.label: bash — reproducible Proxmox operations

  • Application / data / GPU compute separation
  • Encrypted PostgreSQL integration, least privilege
  • Controlled consumption of a remote LLM API
  • Design of persistent workflows
  • Preparing HTTPS publishing behind a reverse proxy
  • Secrets management and exposure surface reduction

git.title: Git — On-Premise AI Portfolio
git.desc: Git — GitHub vs GitLab, the value of a self-hosted GitLab, and repository discipline — portfolio of Stéphane Muraro.
git.subtitle: GitHub · GitLab · repository discipline
git.intro: Git is the foundation of my code work: versioning, preserving history, and above all separating what is public from what is internal. This page covers the GitHub / GitLab nuance, the value of a self-hosted GitLab, and the repository discipline I apply daily.
git.t1: Criterion GitHub GitLabHosting modelSaaS (cloud)SaaS or self-hosted (on-premise)Free editionCloud offeringCommunity Edition — open source, self-installableUse in this projectPublic · training · portfolioInternal · professional codeContinuous integrationGitHub ActionsBuilt-in CI/CD pipelinesDistinctive strengthCommunity, visibilitySovereignty, full control over data
git.why: Why host your own GitLab? Hosting your own GitLab (Community Edition, open source) keeps code and its history outside the cloud: control over access, retention and backups, direct integration with on-premise infrastructure, and consistency with a sovereignty and compliance approach (ISO 27001). GitHub remains ideal for what is meant to be public (portfolio, training); an internal GitLab for what must stay controlled.
git.remote2.list:
• Professional code
  • History kept internal
  • Restricted and traced access
git.isolation: Isolation by architecture: professional code never passes through a public repository. This is not just an organizational rule, it is a structural separation of remotes.
git.t3: File / folderProblemFix.idea/PyCharm configgit rm -r --cached .idea/.venv/Python virtual envgit rm -r --cached .venv/dist/PyInstaller buildgit rm -r --cached dist/*.lnkWindows shortcutsExclude via .gitignore
git.lessons.list:
• Always create the .gitignore before the first git add .
  • The remote repository keeps a copy of the history pushed to it; project backup and restore must be documented separately
  • Store tokens (PAT) in the system's credential manager, never in URLs
  • Only one active remote per project; rename master → main
  • --allow-unrelated-histories to merge two histories with no common ancestor

obs.title: Stéphane Muraro — Obsidian | On-Premise AI Portfolio
obs.desc: Obsidian as a personal knowledge base — note-taking and documentation of the On-Premise AI infrastructure — portfolio of Stéphane Muraro
obs.subtitle: Personal knowledge base — living documentation of the On-Premise AI infrastructure
obs.why: Why Obsidian? When building an AI infrastructure from scratch — Proxmox, GPU passthrough, local LLMs, RAG, Python pipelines — memory is no longer enough. I needed a tool that stores my notes locally, in pure Markdown, with no cloud subscription, and that links concepts together. Obsidian has been the building companion for this entire infrastructure: every command tested, every error encountered, every architecture decision has been logged in a dedicated vault. This portfolio is, in part, the public synthesis of it.
obs.p1.p: Obsidian is a local-first Markdown note editor: files stay on disk, in plain text format. No account required, no data sent to the cloud by default. Its strength lies in the bidirectional link graph ([[wikilink]]) that turns isolated notes into a navigable knowledge network.
obs.p1.list:
• Markdown files stored locally (C:\Notes\infra-vault)
  • Interactive graph of links between concepts
  • Instant full-text search across the whole vault
  • Templates to standardize note-taking
  • Community plugins (Dataview, Kanban, Calendar…)
  • Optional sync via OneDrive or Git
obs.t1: CriterionDecisionData sovereigntyLocal files, zero cloud dependencyLong-lasting formatMarkdown — readable without Obsidian in 10 yearsNo subscriptionFree for personal use (Sync and Publish optional)SpeedLaunches in < 1 s, real-time searchBidirectional linksNaturally link Proxmox ↔ GPU ↔ LLM ↔ DockerExtensibleDataview plugin = SQL-like queries on notes
obs.p3.h: Concrete role in building the infrastructure
obs.p3.intro: The infra-vault vault has accompanied every stage of the project, from the technology watch phase to the writing of this portfolio. Here are the uses that really made a difference:
obs.p3a.p: One note per work session: goal, commands tested, errors encountered, solution adopted. Essential for resuming a task after several days off without losing context.
obs.p3a.label: markdown — illustrative example of a session note (does not describe the current platform)
obs.p3b.p: Every infrastructure component has its own dedicated note, linked via wikilinks. The Obsidian graph visualizes dependencies in real time: Proxmox → LLM VM → Docker → Ollama → Open WebUI.
obs.p3c.p: Articles, model benchmarks, comparisons (LLaMA vs Mistral vs Phi), reading notes on RAG and Qdrant. All centralized, retrievable in 3 seconds via full-text search.
obs.p4.p: Obsidian's graph view visually connects notes: each dot is a note, each line a link. It reveals thematic clusters (infrastructure, AI, DevOps…) and the vault's central notes.
obs.p4.caption: Knowledge graph — 200+ linked notes, colored by folder.
obs.p5.label: tree — Obsidian vault dedicated to the infrastructure
obs.p5.notes: Golden rule: every technical note in 02-infrastructure/ or 03-ia/ ends with a ## References section listing the URLs consulted — exactly like the pages of this portfolio.

obs.p9.h: From the Obsidian vault to this portfolio
obs.p9.intro: This portfolio was not written from scratch. Each HTML page is the publishable version of an existing Obsidian note, enriched and formatted. The workflow is simple:

obs.p9.adv: Key advantage: the Obsidian note remains the source of truth. If a config changes (Proxmox version, updated LLM model), the note is updated first, then the HTML page is synced.
obs.p9.priv: This flow also keeps unpublished information in the vault (API keys, internal IP addresses, sensitive debug notes) with no risk of exposing it on GitHub.

devops.intro: Operating the platform relies on a chain of free tools — open source software, or fair-code / source-available when the license requires it. The goal is reproducibility (templates, cloning, snapshots), reversibility (backups, rollback) and orchestration (n8n, scripts), with no cloud dependency. Components whose license is not an OSI-approved open source license are flagged as such.

img.synth: Strategic synthesis. The Linux AI node (VM210) now runs ComfyUI 0.36.0 alongside Ollama, on the same RTX 5090 (32 GB), for local photorealistic image generation. The model used is RealVisXL V5.0 FP16 (a photorealism-oriented SDXL derivative), which produced portraits at 512×512 and 1,024×1,024. The central trade-off is sharing a single, exclusive GPU between image generation and LLM inference: coexistence was observed and unloading models without stopping the servers was verified, but automatic request sharing still needs to be built (manual switching for now). Maturity: active on the target (VM210, Linux), distinct from the earlier Windows POC (VM260), which had tried out SDXL/Flux workflows.
img.arch.p1: ComfyUI 0.36.0 runs in a locally built Docker image on VM210: Python base pinned by digest, sources pinned by commit, dependencies locked with their hashes (wheels downloaded then installed offline). Validated environment: Python 3.12.14, PyTorch 2.11.0, CUDA 13.0. Container and cache-fix details on the Docker page.
img.arch.p2: Alternative actually explored: an earlier Windows POC (VM260) had tried out ComfyUI via Docker Desktop with SDXL / Flux workflows. This Linux deployment (VM210) is distinct from it and has not yet confirmed Flux usage; only RealVisXL was used and measured here. Since the RTX 5090 is exclusive, VM210 and VM260 do not use it at the same time.
img.arch.p3: Hardening choices made: unprivileged execution, read-only root filesystem, models mounted read-only, custom and API nodes disabled (without blocking outbound network in general), interface published on loopback only (access via SSH tunnel, no Internet publication).
img.cmd.intro: Account, host and path names replaced with examples. No secret is required. Container and API verification (docker inspect/logs, ollama ps, curl) detailed on the Docker page; GPU telemetry and checkpoint SHA-256 verification on the AI & LLM page.
img.cmd.ssh.label: Reproducible check — accessing the interface via SSH tunnel (from PowerShell, client machine)
img.cmd.ssh.note: Then open http://127.0.0.1:8188/ on that machine. Terminal silence after authentication is normal: -N opens the tunnel without a remote session. Ctrl+C closes the tunnel but does not stop ComfyUI; an unreachable interface after closing the terminal is therefore not necessarily a server failure.
img.diff.p1: Symptom: a graph mixing the RealVisXL checkpoint with SD3/AuraFlow nodes was built then discarded (graph incompatibility). A generation cancellation then got stuck, without an exact cause being established; a targeted restart of the container was needed to return to a healthy state. Solution adopted: back to an adapted SDXL graph (consistent with RealVisXL), which then worked normally.
img.diff.p2: A second incident, described on the Docker page, affected container startup (getpass.getuser() failing for lack of a known UID); it was fixed with environment variables without rebuilding the image.
img.proof.label: session observations — RealVisXL generation (not a benchmark)
img.proof.notes: These are session observations, with no statistical protocol or guarantee of latency or quality. Anatomical realism, poses and quality at scale remain to be evaluated — a successful portrait is not enough to validate these criteria. GPU coexistence measurements (VRAM shared with Ollama, memory release) on the AI & LLM page.
img.limits:
• Automatic request sharing between ComfyUI and Ollama still needs to be built (manual switching for now)
  • Anatomical realism, poses and quality at scale remain to be evaluated
  • Use of Flux on this Linux target is not confirmed — only RealVisXL was measured here
  • Agentic/n8n integrations, shared request admission and the restart-after-reboot policy remain open work
  • RealVisXL V5.0 is released under the Open RAIL++ license: available weights do not mean the absence of license restrictions

gpu.diag.p1: The setup required distinguishing several diagnostic levels, so that each effect could be attributed to a single parameter:
gpu.diag.list:
• firmware and IOMMU
  • host driver and PCIe groups
  • reservation of the GPU and its audio function to vfio-pci
  • VM configuration
  • guest driver and CUDA
  • containerized runtime (GPU access all the way into Docker)
gpu.diag.p2: Before any firmware update, the settings required for IOMMU and VFIO are saved and a rollback is prepared; after any change, IOMMU groups, GPU reservation and VM startup are revalidated. A separate virtual console is kept for recovery.
gpu.diag.notes: Not shown here: no one-off workaround (OVMF patch, hypervisor masking, particular IOMMU mapping…) is displayed until an exact public proof is available. Validating VFIO, the guest driver and CUDA does not allow them to be inferred.
infra.bios.note: The other BIOS values (Above 4G Decoding, Re-Size BAR, Secure Boot…) are not published: only IOMMU activation is attested (see GPU / VFIO). A working passthrough does not replace a dated BIOS report.
